results.result: The authors identified and characterized multiple novel anion-conducting channelrhodopsins (ACRs) from diverse taxa, including MsACR1 from Mantoniella squamata, GpACR1 from Goniomonas pacifica, S16-ACR1 from an uncultured MAST3 stramenopile, TaraACR3 from haptophytes, and TaraACR1/TaraACR2 from giant viruses. These ACRs represent multiple ChR subfamilies, some from previously unexplored clades.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 collectively describe the phylogenetic diversity and taxonomic origins of the identified ACRs. The phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1A) and sequence identification methods are clearly described, with appropriate citations and genomic/metagenomic sources documented. The classification is supported by both sequence analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction.

results.result: Electrophysiological characterization revealed that all tested constructs are anion-conducting channelrhodopsins with varying photocurrent properties. MsACR1 exhibited a redshifted λmax at 555 nm compared to other ACRs (470-510 nm), with photocurrent amplitudes up to 10 nA and off-kinetics ranging from 3 ms (TaraACR2) to 400 ms (GpACR1). Light sensitivity was proportional to off-kinetics, with MsACR1, GpACR1, and TaraACR3 showing high sensitivity (half-maximal activation at 20-40 µW/mm²).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C58 describe comprehensive electrophysiological characterization with data shown in Figure 1B-F and Appendix figures. The ion selectivity experiments (C57-C58) appropriately demonstrate anion conductance through ion substitution experiments. Sample sizes are reported (n=4-12), and the measurements follow standard patch-clamp methodology. The relationship between kinetics and light sensitivity (C54) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Systematic mutagenesis of residues near the β-ionone ring of MsACR1 revealed that most substitutions (G186P, G186C, G186H, G186T, and mutations mimicking RubyACRs) resulted in blue-shifts rather than red-shifts. The F138N mutation showed a small redshift but strongly increased τoff. Mutations near the retinal Schiff base (F185Y, T87A) also affected spectral properties and kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C73 describe mutagenesis results shown in Figure 2D-F. The data are clearly presented with appropriate controls (wild-type comparison). The finding that β-ionone ring mutations cause blue-shifts is counterintuitive but well-documented. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3-7 for mutants), though the manuscript notes this is surprising and discusses potential structural explanations.

results.result: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 (raACR) shifted λmax 20 nm toward red light (from 555 to 575 nm), reduced τoff fivefold, shifted half-maximal activity from 605 to 635 nm, and increased photocurrent amplitude at 690 nm twofold compared to wild-type. This mutant exhibited 19-fold larger photocurrent at 690 nm compared to GtACR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80, C3-C5 describe the key raACR mutation and its effects. The data are shown in Figure 2B-F and Appendix figures with clear quantification. The comparison to Chrimson's A298 residue (C74) provides rational design basis. The 19-fold improvement over GtACR1 (C80) is a strong comparative result, though it would be strengthened by direct side-by-side measurements under identical conditions.

results.result: MsACR1 and raACR expressed well in hippocampal neurons with proper membrane localization and no aggregation. Both ACRs effectively suppressed neuronal spiking at very low light intensities, with MsACR1 showing 25% spike reduction at just 5 nW/mm² and both achieving 30-90% reduction at 100-7100 nW/mm². Complete silencing was achieved during continuous illumination.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87, C26-C27 describe in vitro neuronal characterization shown in Figure 3A-C. The expression data (confocal imaging) and functional data (patch-clamp recordings) are well-documented. The extremely low light sensitivity (5 nW/mm²) is a notable finding. However, the range of 30-90% reduction (C86) is quite broad and could benefit from more precise quantification or explanation of variability.

results.result: Light-evoked onset spikes were observed for both ACRs during continuous illumination, attributed to chloride efflux in axonal compartments. Soma-targeted versions (st-MsACR1 and st-raACR) were engineered using Kv2.1 targeting sequences, which significantly reduced onset spike probability, particularly for st-raACR under pulsed illumination.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 describe the onset spike phenomenon and mitigation strategy shown in Figure 3D and Appendix 1-figure 7. The mechanistic explanation (C89) is appropriately attributed to prior literature (Mahn et al., 2016). The soma-targeting approach is rational, though C94 notes only a "trend" for st-MsACR1, suggesting incomplete mitigation. Statistical significance is reported for st-raACR (C93).

results.result: Under pulsed illumination, MsACR1 nearly completely shunted all spikes independent of light color, while raACR showed lower potency but superior temporal resolution. raACR allowed 50% spike recovery at 50 ms post-silencing compared to 180 ms for MsACR1, demonstrating raACR's higher temporal resolution for optogenetic applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99, C8, C28 describe comparative performance shown in Figure 3E-G. The temporal resolution data (C98-C99) are clearly quantified and represent a key functional difference between the variants. The interpretation that raACR's lower potency is due to reduced ion flux per photocycle (C97) is reasonable but remains an inference. The data support the conclusion that raACR offers better temporal control.

results.result: Monte Carlo simulations using in vitro light titration data predicted that MsACR1 and raACR would silence larger brain volumes compared to commonly used optogenetic inhibitors Jaws and GtACR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 describe computational modeling shown in Appendix 1-figure 8. The Monte Carlo approach is appropriate for modeling light penetration and is properly cited (Stujenske et al., 2015). However, the simulation relies on in vitro measurements and tissue optical properties, which may not fully capture in vivo complexity. The comparison to Jaws and GtACR1 provides useful context but would be strengthened by experimental validation.

results.result: In vivo experiments in mouse primary motor cortex (M1) demonstrated that both MsACR1 and raACR induced immediate locomotion arrest upon 635 nm illumination at 20 Hz. Both ACRs showed homogeneous expression without cell death, and activation led to significantly reduced velocity, with MsACR1 showing more substantial effects than raACR.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107, C6-C7 describe in vivo behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4. The histological validation (C104) and behavioral quantification (C105-C107) are appropriate. The interpretation that MsACR1's stronger effect is due to longer-lasting response (C107) is reasonable given the kinetic data. However, complete locomotion arrest is a complex phenotype that may involve multiple circuit mechanisms beyond simple inhibition.

results.result: Cell-type-specific expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons with simultaneous optrode recordings revealed complex network responses to ACR activation. At 10 mW, raACR showed superior inhibition compared to MsACR1, modulating >90% of units with both blue and red light, while MsACR1 affected >75% of units with red light. Both ACRs significantly decreased running speed at 10 mW red light, with no effect in GFP controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C117 describe sophisticated in vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5. The experimental design appropriately addresses circuit complexity by targeting specific cell types. The quantification of unit responses using Z-scores is appropriate, though the 2-fold SD threshold (C111-C112) is somewhat arbitrary. The finding that raACR is more effective at high power (C114) contrasts with in vitro results and deserves further investigation. Control experiments (C117) are essential and properly conducted.

results.result: MsACR1 from Mantoniella squamata, a member of the prasinophyte ACR family, exhibited the most red-shifted activation among screened ACRs with λmax at 555 nm, showing high sensitivity to yellow-green light.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C23, C51, C22 describe the initial identification and key spectral property of MsACR1. The λmax measurement is clearly shown in Figure 1B-C with appropriate methodology. The classification as a prasinophyte ACR is supported by phylogenetic analysis (C22). This represents the starting point for the engineering work.

results.result: Both MsACR1 and raACR reliably shunt neuronal spiking in vitro and induce motor arrest in vivo using 635 nm light. Complete shunting was achieved during continuous illumination, with onset spikes minimized by pulsed illumination and soma targeting. Pulsed illumination was more efficient for MsACR1 due to slower kinetics, while raACR's faster kinetics enabled higher temporal resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143, C146-C148 synthesize key functional findings. The data supporting these conclusions are presented throughout Figures 3-4. The recommendation for pulsed illumination and soma targeting (C146) is well-justified by the data. The mechanistic explanations for differential efficiency (C147-C148) are reasonable inferences from the kinetic measurements.

results.result: MsACR1 and raACR show minimal photocurrent inactivation during continuous illumination and can be reactivated instantly without decline, unlike other commonly used ACRs. Combined with good expression, high chloride conductance, and slow off-kinetics, these properties enable inhibition at light intensities as low as 20 nW/mm², making them valuable additions to the optogenetic toolbox for long-lasting inhibition in large brain volumes.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C158 represent the authors' overall conclusions about the utility of these tools. The lack of photocurrent inactivation (C153-C154) is clearly demonstrated in the electrophysiology data. The 20 nW/mm² sensitivity (C157) is supported by Figure 3C. The conclusion about utility (C158) is reasonable given the comprehensive characterization, though "valuable addition" is somewhat subjective. The comparison to other ACRs (C153) would be strengthened by direct side-by-side measurements.

results.result: The authors speculate that wild-type MsACR1 may be useful for studying algal phototaxis, as both ACRs and CCRs may cooperate to regulate photo-orientation in motile prasinophytes, and M. squamata possesses both proton-conducting CCR1 and chloride-conducting MsACR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are speculative about potential basic biology applications. While the presence of both channel types in M. squamata is documented (C121 cites Govorunova et al., 2021), the functional cooperation hypothesis (C120) is cited to prior work but remains untested. This represents interesting future directions but is not experimentally validated in the current manuscript.

results.result: TaraACR1 and TaraACR2, identified as viral rhodopsins from giant viruses, were well-expressed and showed large photocurrents compared to some previously characterized viral rhodopsin channels. TaraACR2 exhibited fast off-kinetics comparable to ZipACR and RapACR.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 describe the viral ACRs. The viral origin is supported by sequence analysis (C123), and the functional characterization (C125-C126) is shown in Figure 1. The comparison to other viral rhodopsins and fast ACRs is appropriately cited. These represent interesting additions to the viral rhodopsin repertoire, though they were not the focus of detailed characterization.

results.result: GpACR1 and S16-ACR1 are unsuitable for optogenetic applications due to their photocurrent properties but reveal interesting molecular features. GpACR1 shows a secondary peak upon light shut-off indicative of photointermediate back-isomerization, while S16-ACR1 exhibits voltage-dependent inactivation and inward rectification similar to MerMAIDs.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 assess two ACRs as unsuitable for applications but scientifically interesting. The photocurrent characteristics are clearly shown in Figure 1D. The mechanistic interpretations (C129, C131) are appropriately cautious ("expected," "may offer insight") and cite relevant literature. The assessment of unsuitability (C127) is reasonable given the data, though these proteins could still have niche applications.

results.result: The action spectrum of MsACR1 shows highest activity in yellow-green light with a distinct blue-light peak, likely from β-band absorption. Surprisingly, most β-ionone ring substitutions caused blue-shifts, possibly due to high existing polarity or ring twisting. The retinal Schiff base region was more susceptible to modification, with the S218A mutation mimicking red-light-absorbing ChRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C140 discuss spectral tuning mechanisms. The action spectrum data (C132) are clear. The interpretation of the blue peak (C133) is appropriately cited. The unexpected blue-shifts from β-ionone mutations (C134) are well-documented but the mechanistic explanations (C136) remain speculative. The comparison to Chrimson and animal rhodopsins (C138-C140) provides useful context with appropriate citations.

results.result: The authors discuss strategies for optimizing ACR performance, noting that onset spikes require longer photon exposure and can be reduced with shorter/ramped pulses. They speculate that slowing raACR kinetics could improve efficiency, suggesting T87A/T87S mutations or screening DC pair homologs as potential approaches, though most tested mutations that slowed kinetics also blue-shifted λmax.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145, C149-C152 represent discussion of optimization strategies. The inference about onset spike mechanisms (C144) is reasonably based on cited literature. However, the suggestions for improving raACR (C149-C152) are speculative and not experimentally tested. The constraint that kinetic slowing often causes blue-shifts (C150) is documented but limits the proposed strategies. These represent reasonable future directions but lack experimental validation.

results.result: MsACR1 from Mantoniella squamata is a red-shifted anion-conducting channelrhodopsin with peak sensitivity at 555 nm, making it the most red-shifted among the screened ChRs and considerably more red-shifted than most other tested ChRs (λmax 470-510 nm).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a major strength: 'The authors were able to identify a new class of anion conducting channelrhodopsin and have variants that respond strongly to lights with wavelength >550 nm.' The spectral characterization is described as 'solid' and 'very detailed' with no challenges to the λmax measurements.

results.result: The S218A mutation in MsACR1 (creating raACR) produces a 20 nm red-shift toward longer wavelengths (shifting half-maximal activity from 605 to 635 nm) and accelerates photocurrent kinetics by reducing τoff fivefold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers identify this as 'the second major strength of the study' - the development of a red-shifted mutant with faster kinetics from a single mutation. The biophysical characterization is described as 'solid' and 'very detailed' with no challenges to these specific measurements.

results.result: Both MsACR1 and raACR suppress neuronal activity in vitro at very low light intensities, with MsACR1 decreasing spiking probability by 25% at just 5 nW/mm² and achieving strong suppression at >200 nW/mm², with activity reduced to 30-90% at 100-7100 nW/mm².
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the ACRs are very light sensitive and allow for efficient in vitro inhibition of neurons in the nano Watt/mm² range' and describe the in vitro characterization as 'very detailed' and 'solid.' No concerns are raised about these specific in vitro measurements.

results.result: Both MsACR1 and raACR function as optical silencers in vivo, with 635 nm light illumination causing immediate locomotion arrest and significantly reduced velocity in mice expressing these constructs in M1 cortex.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise major concerns: 'the evidence supporting the use of the tools in vivo is incomplete and missing proper controls,' 'critical in vivo control experiments, such as negative controls like GFP or positive controls like NpHR, are missing,' and 'the in vivo experiments did not confirm whether the observed inhibition of mouse locomotion occurred due to the inhibition of neurons or experimental artifacts.' Statistical concerns are also noted regarding animal numbers.

results.result: raACR offers higher temporal resolution than MsACR1, enabling spike triggering with 50% frequency at 50 ms post-illumination compared to 180 ms for MsACR1, due to its accelerated kinetics.
results.evaluation: The temporal resolution advantage is acknowledged as part of the 'second major strength' and the in vitro characterization is described as 'very detailed.' Reviewers note the faster kinetics as a key feature without challenging the temporal resolution measurements.

results.result: raACR shows lower potency for spike suppression compared to MsACR1 under all conditions, likely due to reduced ion flux during a single photocycle, with MsACR1 showing more substantial effects on velocity in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly question this finding: 'From the data shown, the red-shifted raACR work much less efficiently than MsACR1 even with 635 nm light illumination both in vivo (Figure 4D) and in vitro (Figure 3E) despite the 20 nm red-shift. This is inconsistent with the benefits and effects of red-shifting the spectrum in raACR.' They request additional experiments to support the kinetic explanation.

results.result: Both MsACR1 and raACR completely silence current-evoked spiking during continuous illumination in vitro.
results.evaluation: This is part of the in vitro characterization that reviewers describe as 'very detailed' and 'solid' with no specific challenges to the continuous illumination silencing data.

results.result: Light-evoked onset spikes occur at the start of illumination due to chloride efflux in axonal compartments, but can be minimized through pulsed illumination and soma-targeting strategies (st-MsACR1 and st-raACR).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the onset spike phenomenon and note that 'the authors used soma-targeted (st) MsACR1 and raACR for some of their in vitro characterization yielding more efficient inhibition and reduction of co-incidental "on-set" spiking.' The in vitro data on this is accepted, though they note st-variants were not used in initial in vivo experiments.

results.result: Monte Carlo simulations comparing MsACR1 and raACR with other optogenetic inhibitors (Jaws and GtACR1) demonstrate the superiority of MsACR1 and raACR for silencing larger brain volumes.
results.evaluation: While reviewers note that 'benchmarking against other inhibitory tools is somewhat missing' and request 'more parallel comparison with gtACR1, ZipACR and RubyACR in identical conditions,' they do acknowledge in the second review that 'The authors added Supl Fig. 8 in which light power density and propagation of photons... was calculated.' However, the lack of direct experimental comparisons remains a concern.

results.result: In vivo electrophysiology in PV-Cre mice shows that raACR produces superior inhibition at 10 mW (>90% of units modulated) compared to MsACR1, with complex changes in neuronal firing including both inhibition and disinhibition, and significant decreases in running speed at 10 mW red light.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note in the second review: 'They added a new set of experiments in Fig.5 in which PV neurons were exclusively targeted. However, the authors show in vivo electrophysiology demonstrating the expected inhibition of firing neurons (presumably PV neurons expressing raACR) under 635 nm light and disinhibition (presumably excitatory neurons).' This addresses previous concerns about in vivo validation.

results.result: Control animals injected with hSyn1-DIO-eGFP show no significant change in running speed upon illumination, validating the specificity of the optogenetic effects.
results.evaluation: While reviewers initially criticized the lack of controls, they acknowledge in the second review that control experiments were added, though they note 'The authors have not added control experiments in Fig 4 yet but plan to conduct them later.' The GFP control data presented is accepted as valid.

results.result: The screening identified multiple novel ACRs from diverse and previously unexplored clades, including GpACR1 (from cryptomonad Goniomonas pacifica, related to labyrinthulean ACRs), S16-ACR1 (from MAST3 stramenopile forming its own clade), TaraACR3 (haptophyte), and viral ACRs TaraACR1/2 forming a separate subfamily.
results.evaluation: The phylogenetic characterization and identification of novel ACRs is part of the 'solid' biophysical characterization acknowledged by reviewers. No specific challenges are raised to the taxonomic classifications or phylogenetic relationships.

results.result: MsACR1, TaraACR1, and TaraACR2 show minimal photocurrent inactivation during continuous illumination and can be reactivated instantly without decline, unlike TaraACR3, S16-ACR1, and GpACR1 which show considerable inactivation.
results.evaluation: This is part of the detailed in vitro biophysical characterization that reviewers describe as 'solid' and 'very detailed.' The lack of photocurrent inactivation is implicitly accepted as a strength for optogenetic applications.

results.result: Ion selectivity experiments demonstrate that all tested ChRs are anion-conducting (ACRs), as only replacement of external Cl⁻ (not Na⁺) caused photocurrent changes and shifted reversal potential close to the Nernst potential of Cl⁻.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'the evidence for the spectral confirmation and biophysical characterization of MsACR and raACR, and ion selectivity are solid.' No challenges are raised to the ion selectivity data.

results.result: Mutagenesis of the β-ionone ring region in MsACR1 unexpectedly resulted in blue-shifts rather than red-shifts, including mutations at position 186 (G186P, G186C, G186H, G186T) and mutations mimicking RubyACR residues (W142Y, W182Q, G186I).
results.evaluation: This is part of the detailed mutagenesis characterization. While reviewers request more data on kinetics and illumination protocols, they do not challenge the spectral shift measurements from these mutations.

results.result: MsACR1-S218A (raACR) exhibits a 19-fold larger photocurrent at 690 nm compared to GtACR1, the most commonly used ACR for optogenetic applications.
results.evaluation: While the measurement itself is not challenged, reviewers note 'There are limited comparisons to existing variants of ACRs under the same conditions in the manuscript overall. There should be more parallel comparison with gtACR1, ZipACR and RubyACR in identical conditions.' The lack of comprehensive benchmarking weakens confidence in superiority claims.

results.result: Both MsACR1 and raACR show good membrane expression in neurons without intracellular aggregation or cell death, with homogeneous expression visible in somatic, axonal, and dendritic compartments.
results.evaluation: Expression quality is part of the accepted in vitro characterization. Reviewers note 'the ACRs are well expressed' as part of the strengths, with no challenges to the expression or localization data.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on phylogenetic diversity and taxonomic classification (C29-C38). Both evaluations support the phylogenetic characterization as solid with no challenges to the taxonomic classifications or phylogenetic relationships.

Strong agreement on initial identification and spectral properties of MsACR1 (C2, C23, C51). Both acknowledge this as a major strength with solid spectral characterization and no challenges to λmax measurements.

Strong agreement on the raACR mutation and red-shift achievement (C3, C4, C76-C78). Both identify this as a major strength with solid biophysical characterization, though OpenEval notes the 19-fold improvement could be strengthened by direct comparisons.

Strong agreement on in vitro neuronal characterization and light sensitivity (C27, C84-C86). Both describe the in vitro data as solid and detailed, acknowledging nano Watt/mm² range sensitivity. OpenEval notes the broad 30-90% reduction range.

Strong agreement on electrophysiological characterization and lack of photocurrent inactivation (C40-C48, C153-C154). Both evaluations support the comprehensive patch-clamp data and accept this as a strength for optogenetic applications.
Strong agreement on ion selectivity (C57-C58). Both evaluations explicitly support the anion conductance demonstration through ion substitution experiments as solid evidence.
Strong agreement on temporal resolution advantages (C8, C28, C98-C99). Both acknowledge faster kinetics and better temporal control as key features with detailed in vitro support.

Strong agreement on onset spike phenomenon and soma-targeting mitigation (C88-C89, C92-C93). Both accept the in vitro data on onset spikes and soma-targeted variants yielding more efficient inhibition.

Strong agreement on in vivo electrophysiology with PV neuron targeting (C110-C116). Both support the sophisticated experimental design and acknowledge the new Figure 5 data demonstrating expected inhibition and disinhibition patterns.

Agreement on control experiments (C117). OpenEval notes controls as essential and properly conducted; peer reviewers acknowledge control experiments were added in revision, though some remain planned for future work.

Agreement on mutagenesis results and spectral shifts (C61-C65, C134). Both support the spectral shift measurements from β-ionone ring mutations, though OpenEval notes the counterintuitive blue-shifts and peer reviewers request more kinetics data.

Major disagreement on in vivo behavioral experiments (C6-C7, C105-C107). OpenEval supports the data as appropriate; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN citing incomplete evidence, missing controls (GFP, NpHR), and concerns about whether inhibition is neuronal or artifactual.

Disagreement on comparative performance and kinetic explanations (C96-C97, C107). OpenEval supports the interpretation that raACR's lower potency is due to reduced ion flux; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting raACR works less efficiently than MsACR1 even at 635 nm, inconsistent with red-shift benefits.

Partial disagreement on computational modeling and benchmarking (C100-C101). OpenEval supports the Monte Carlo approach but notes lack of experimental validation; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing missing parallel comparisons with gtACR1, ZipACR, and RubyACR under identical conditions.

Partial disagreement on superiority claims (C80). OpenEval supports the 19-fold improvement but notes it would be strengthened by direct comparisons; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN due to limited comparisons under identical conditions, weakening confidence in superiority claims.
Agreement on expression quality (C83). Both evaluations support that ACRs are well expressed with good membrane localization as part of the in vitro characterization strengths.
Agreement on continuous illumination silencing (C87, C142). Both support this as part of the detailed in vitro characterization with no specific challenges to the data.
Agreement on onset spike mitigation recommendations (C143). Both support the pulsed illumination and soma-targeting recommendations based on the data presented.
Agreement on mechanistic explanations for differential efficiency (C148). Both support the kinetic-based explanations as reasonable inferences from the temporal resolution measurements.

Partial overlap on overall utility conclusions (C141). OpenEval supports the synthesis of functional findings; peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating on in vivo experiments tempers confidence in the complete utility assessment.
Agreement on lack of photocurrent inactivation as a key feature (C153-C154). Both evaluations support this characteristic as well-demonstrated and valuable for optogenetic applications.

OpenEval rates speculative basic biology applications (C119-C122) as UNCERTAIN, noting functional cooperation hypothesis is untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative claims.
OpenEval supports viral ACR characterization (C123-C126) as interesting additions to viral rhodopsin repertoire. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these viral variants.
OpenEval supports assessment of two ACRs as unsuitable for applications but scientifically interesting (C127-C131). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these variants.

Partial overlap on spectral tuning mechanisms (C132-C140, C134). OpenEval supports the data but notes mechanistic explanations remain speculative; peer reviewers support the measurements but request more data on kinetics and illumination protocols.

OpenEval rates optimization strategies (C144-C145, C149-C152) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative and not experimentally tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these future optimization suggestions.
